metadata.title: A new macroeconomic measure of human capital exploiting PISA and PIAAC: Linking education policies to productivity (EN)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This OECD working paper constructs macroeconomic human-capital measures by linking PISA student test scores (for 15-year-olds) to PIAAC adult test scores (for working-age cohorts) and then aggregating across cohorts using cohort population shares. The analysis is conducted at the country level (and in some specifications as a country-time panel), using regression-based estimation of elasticities and subsequent construction of a human-capital stock; it does not report student-level microdata estimation steps that would require applying PISA/PIAAC sampling weights. Because the paper’s empirical strategy is macroeconomic (productivity regressions and stock construction) rather than a direct re-estimation of ILSA item/scale models, the manuscript does not specify any PISA/PIAAC complex-survey weight variables (e.g., W_FSTUWT) or replicate-weight procedures. For analysts wishing to reproduce or extend the work with microdata, appropriate ILSA sampling weights and replicate methods would need to be applied when estimating student- or adult-level score models, but this paper’s reported results are based on already-constructed test-score series and macro regressions.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper does not perform student-level estimation of PV-based achievement outcomes; instead, it uses already-constructed adult and student test-score series (and extends PISA series via external linking) to estimate macro elasticities and build a cohort-weighted human-capital stock. As a result, plausible-value generation/combining rules are not part of the reported methodology. Missing-data handling is also not described because the study relies on availability of country-level test-score series across waves/cohorts and on constructed time-series links (e.g., interpolation and backcasting), rather than reporting an imputation strategy for micro-level missing responses.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The paper uses country-level time series constructed from PISA student test scores (Reading, Mathematics, Science for 15-year-olds) and PIAAC adult test scores (literacy, numeracy, problem solving) matched by 5-year age cohorts. For the matching/elasticity estimation, it relies on the subset of countries for which both PIAAC and extended/backcast PISA series are available (35 countries for the correlation/matching exercise; 34 countries in some regression specifications with country fixed effects). For the human-capital stock construction, it computes two variants: a comprehensive stock for the working-age population (16–65) using all 10 cohorts, available for 15 OECD countries (mostly with series starting in the mid-2000s), and a shorter-horizon stock for ages 16–39 using the first five cohorts, available for 54 countries in the latest year. For PISA time series gaps between test years, the paper fills gaps using linear interpolation; for backcasting prior to 2000, it uses linked earlier international test-score vintages from the World Bank Global Dataset on Education Quality (Altinok et al., 2018).

data.outcome_summary: This OECD working paper develops a new macroeconomic measure of human capital that combines the quantity of education (mean years of schooling) with the quality of education (student test scores) and links these to adult skills measured by PIAAC. The core methodological step estimates elasticities by regressing adult test scores for matched cohorts on earlier student test scores (extended/backcast PISA series) and mean years of schooling, allowing the quality elasticity to differ from the quantity elasticity. Using these estimated elasticities, the paper constructs a cohort-weighted human-capital stock for the working-age population (16–65) and a shorter-horizon alternative (16–39) when longer series are unavailable. The resulting human-capital stock is then used in productivity regressions within the OECD QASR framework, including cross-country time-series panel models for OECD countries and purely cross-sectional models for a larger set of countries. The paper reports that the new human-capital measure is robustly positively associated with multi-factor productivity and that simulated improvements in student test scores (quality) imply larger long-run productivity gains than comparable increases in mean years of schooling (quantity), while emphasizing very long lags from education reforms to macroeconomic effects.
